entry.title: Why I built a self-hosted booking platform instead of using SaaS tools
entry.summary:
I’ve spent years building websites and small platforms where booking functionality was needed. Over time, I realized I was either rebuilding the same foundations again and again or relying on hosted platforms and plugin-heavy CMS setups that I didn’t fully control. So I decided to build a self-hosted booking and website system that I could actually own, extend, and reuse across projects. Some deliberate choices I made:
• No plugin-based architecture
• Full control over data and hosting
• Modular structure that can grow beyond a single use case It started as an internal tool for accommodation websites and slowly evolved into a production-ready system. I’m curious how other developers here approach similar problems: I’m also curious how other developers here approach sharing or distributing similar self-hosted tools — especially when they’re not SaaS products. If anyone is curious, the system I built for this is called BellaVista. You can find more details here: https://bellavistaproject.eu Looking forward to hearing your thoughts.

entry.title: Linux Fundamentals - Part 2: Understanding Directory Hierarchy
entry.summary:
This post summarizes what I have learned about the most common Linux directories and how they are used in a typical system. / - Root Directory /bin - Binaries ls cd cp mv rm /dev - Device Files /dev/null
This line of code can be sent to destroy any file or string. /dev/zero
This line of code contains an infinite sequence of 0. /dev/random
This line of code contains an infinite sequence of random values. /etc - Configuration Files /usr - User System Resources /usr/bin - contains basic user commands. ‘/usr/sbin’ - contains additional commands for the administrator. ‘/usr/lib’ - contains the system libraries. /usr/share’ - contains documentation manual pages. /home - User Home Directories /home/Downloads
/lib - Shared Libraries These directories store shared libraries required by system binaries in /bin and /sbin. They are essential for the system to boot and function properly.

entry.title: Why I Built a GitHub Roaster That "Melts" Your Browser (And How I Did It)
entry.summary:
The Hook
Most developer tools are built to be "safe." They have clean lines, predictable buttons, and a sense of order. At @AvyroxSolutions, we decided to do the opposite. We built Vokrix—a GitHub analyzer that doesn't just roast your code; it tries to break your reality. The Vision: Atmospheric Engineering
We wanted to move beyond the "SaaS dashboard" aesthetic. By implementing a Dynamic Theme & Localized Identity engine, we created a platform that shifts based on "Moods". Hacker Mode: High-contrast terminal green with mechanical keyboard haptics. Chaos Mode: A violent red theme that triggers a "Reality Breach" using horizontal screen tearing and VHS scanlines. The Technical Deep Dive: The "Melt" and the "Breach"
To make the CHAOS mode feel visceral, we used a combination of: SVG Gooey Filters: We used feGaussianBlur and feColorMatrix to make the logo literally "bleed" and melt when the system enters a critical state. State-Driven Soundscapes: We synced industrial hums and digital whines to the generation logic to create sensory overload. The Hidden Command: We implemented a global listener for a specific keyboard sequence—"BREAK"—which triggers a simulated kernel panic and reveals a hidden technical cheat sheet. Why Psychological UX Matters
As engineers at Avyrox Solutions, we believe the best way to prove you can handle a client's complex infrastructure is to show you have absolute control over your own UI. If we can safely simulate a "system failure" that scares the user, imagine what we can do for your actual uptime. The Challenge
I’ve opened a private beta for the next 24 hours. I want to see if you can find the backdoor and "break" the system to unlock our internal architecture docs. Try it here: https://vokrix.app Check out the team behind it: https://avyrox-solutions.com Discussion for the Comments
How do you feel about "hostile" UI design for marketing? What’s the coolest SVG filter trick you’ve seen lately? Did you find the BREAK command? (No spoilers!)

entry.summary: Railway, a San Francisco-based cloud platform that has quietly amassed two million developers without spending a dollar on marketing, announced Thursday that it raised $100 million in a Series B funding round, as surging demand for artificial intelligence applications exposes the limitations of legacy cloud infrastructure. TQ Ventures led the round, with participation from FPV Ventures, Redpoint, and Unusual Ventures. The investment values Railway as one of the most significant infrastructure startups to emerge during the AI boom, capitalizing on developer frustration with the complexity and cost of traditional platforms like Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud. entry.title: Hypercore for Hyperliquid Enters Public Beta
entry.summary: Quicknode has released Hypercore for Hyperliquid in public beta, giving builders filtered access to Hyperliquid data via Streams, gRPC, and JSON-RPC.

entry.title: Claude Code costs up to $200 a month. Goose does the same thing for free.
entry.summary: The artificial intelligence coding revolution comes with a catch: it's expensive. Claude Code, Anthropic's terminal-based AI agent that can write, debug, and deploy code autonomously, has captured the imagination of software developers worldwide. But its pricing — ranging from $20 to $200 per month depending on usage — has sparked a growing rebellion among the very programmers it aims to serve. Now, a free alternative is gaining traction. Goose, an open-source AI agent developed by Block (the financial technology company formerly known as Square), offers nearly identical functionality to Claude Code but runs entirely on a user's local machine. entry.title: Listen Labs raises $69M after viral billboard hiring stunt to scale AI customer interviews
entry.summary: Alfred Wahlforss was running out of options. His startup, Listen Labs, needed to hire over 100 engineers, but competing against Mark Zuckerberg's $100 million offers seemed impossible. So he spent $5,000 — a fifth of his marketing budget — on a billboard in San Francisco displaying what looked like gibberish: five strings of random numbers. The numbers were actually AI tokens. Decoded, they led to a coding challenge: build an algorithm to act as a digital bouncer at Berghain, the Berlin nightclub famous for rejecting nearly everyone at the door. Within days, thousands attempted the puzzle. 430 cracked it. Some got hired. The winner flew to Berlin, all expenses paid.
